# Introduction to R

What exactly is R? What are the benefits of using R? What are the downsides relative to SPSS other packages? Note that one can use R in its most basic format or use GUIs that are more "point and click"

## R as a programming environment

R is a programming environment in which researchers can do a variety of different things. Most typically, however, I use R to

1.Manage data sets 2.Clean, code data, create summary scores 3.Do statistical analyses like t-tests, regression, multilevel modeling, SEM 4.Create graphs, tables, and figures 5.Read OSF pages, scrape internet sites, clean up my Google Drive, folders, rename files, etc

# Why R?

-It is Free! -It is open-source which means (I think...) that anyone can access, add to R and its numerous packages -It uses a simple programming language developed by experts, you can see all source code (unlike some proprietary stats packages) -This all means that there are new additions to R all the time to keep up with state-of-the-art changes in statistics

## Why do I like using R?

-I like programming! -I like learning new code, analyses -Saves time and energe- I use R to extract results and create tables that are perfect! -No more missing a decimal or wrong negative sign... -I can download it on my home laptop and direct R to analyze data that is networked -Much faster than trying to cloud access SPSS, Mplus, etc.

# What steps do you take to get started?

1.  Download R from https://cran.r-project.org/
2.  Download RStudio from https://posit.co/downloads

**What is the difference?**

RStudio is technically a *Graphical User Interface* that has more built-in "point and click" options compared to Base R

![R basic](images/Screenshot%202026-08-18%20103303-01.png){fig-align="left" width="479"}

![R Studio](images/Screenshot%202026-08-18%20103627.png){width="526"}

RStudio has subwindows for the 1. Console, 2. Script Editor, 3. Environment, and 4. Files

The main advantage is that there are point and click ways for many of the steps we would use in Basic R Also there is syntax highlighint, code completion, and some smart coding routines

# Packages

There is **Base R** which has a number of **functions**

-Functions are like commands that have built in coded instructions to complete a task -Some are pretty simple: mean(var1) just computes the mean of var1 -Others are much more complicated -lm for example lm(y \~ x1 +x2, data=newdata) -Is a mutiple regression "function" with many built in commands and routines

So while Base R is great and can do MANY things, in fact most of what we want to do in this class...

Programmers develop and distribute **packages** which typically are designed to have routines and functions to carry out specific tasks. Some packages read in data, some are for statistical analysis, some create tables, some can read Google Drive...

Once you install a package using **install.packages()**, you then "load" the package using **library()** -Note that while you only have to install packages once (unless you change computers), you have to load packages ***every time you restart R*** -As you will see, in the *scripts* that I write, I usually have load(haven) at the top along with other packages, that way when I open and run the scripts, that step happens first -If you try to use commands from a package that isn't loaded, you will get an error

``` r
# example code to install a package
install.packages("tidyverse", dependencies = TRUE)

# load package
library(tidyverse)
```

# R Programming Some Basic Terminology

## Objects

R stores data and output in objects.

``` r
A <- 3
B <- "hello"

A
B
```

### Often we will create objects that hold output from a particular analysis

reg1_results \<- lm(y \~ x1 + x2, data=mydata)

reg1_results is an object, that is object is "assigned" (\<-) to include the results of the lm function which is regressin y on x1 and x2 using the data set "mydata"

## Functions

Functions perform most of the work in R.

``` r
log(10)

?seq
```

# Getting Data into R

Most of my experience reading in data has to do with bringing data in from some sort of spreadsheet like in an excel or SPSS file Can also read in data other ways, however

## Vectors

``` r
x <- c(1, 3, 5)

seq(from = 1, to = 7, by = 2)

rep("yes", 2)
```

## Data Frames

Datasets are typically stored in data frames. R will refer to data frames has having ***Rows*** and ***Columns***

Typically in a wide-format dataset, each person/case/subject/participant/unit will represent a row, while each variable will be in a column. It is helpful to remember that terminology because we will sometimes reference columns and rows.

# Many ways to read in data

Most often I end up reading in data from a spreadsheet. Those can be in various ascii formats such as .csv (comma separated), .txt files, .tab files, .dat files which are just text files. Also I often read in SPSS (.sav) files or SAS, STATA and others. Note that those latter files require specialized packages

## Quick Examples - will demo later in the book and course

## Reading CSV Data

A CSV (comma-separated values) file is a common format for storing data.

``` r
school <- read.csv("school.csv")
View(school)
```

- `read.csv()` imports the data file into R.
- `school <-` stores the dataset in an object named `school`.
- `View()` opens the dataset in a spreadsheet-style window.

## Reading SPSS Data with `haven`

The **haven** package imports data files created in SPSS, Stata, and SAS.

``` r
install.packages("haven")
library(haven)

school <- read_sav("school.sav")

View(school)
```

- `library(haven)` loads the haven package.
- `read_sav()` imports an SPSS `.sav` file.
- `school <-` stores the dataset in an object named `school`.
- `View()` opens the dataset in a spreadsheet-style window.

# Data Management

Here I will go through some basic R commands that I use when reading in data and then taking a look, doing some screening, etc

## Subsetting

``` r
school[1, 2]

school[1:2, ]

school$math
```

## Adding Variables

``` r
school$log_math <- log(school$math)
```
